The only tip I know for GMs is, don't railroad your players.

If you wrote a long, carefully-planned adventure but your players insist on going off the rails, you gotta scrap your adventure and come up with something new. The players choose the direction of the story, not the DM, who is really just the narrator.

i'll add to this. have a general outline of the story, and have some NPC's but don't be afraid of the players doing unexpected stuff and going off course. just think how the NPC's would react and consider the RP in the RPG. the players may break your story, but they will have fun doing it. it might be anticlimactic, but that has its own charm.
An important corollary to providing the story is to make choices matter.

Yeah, I generally understood that rule and my plan is to basically dump them into a world with some conflicts in it and let them choose their own path. We already agreed before hand that we will just keep playing till we are bored so having a set storyline isn't a big deal for us.
If you play a game with plenty of rules, such as DND / Pathfinder, make sure you KNOW your rules. If you do not like rules play something lighter, like Paranoia or the Firefly RPG.

Know what your players want, and try to provide it. Do they want mostly dialog and story telling? Or a lot of set-piece battles? Do they want a hard, tactical fight, where if they mess it up their characters perma-die? Or do they want a kinder, gentler approach, where exploitation of the rules is discouraged? As a player, I've had very good times with both, but not at the same time.

Some of the best times I've had have been when I role-played counter to the party's best interest. For example, my character lacked tact, or took offense and behaved badly. But if wrong moves yield perma-death, no one is going to roll-play getting drunk and starting a bar-fight. On the other hand, no one is going to be planning battles like chess games, unless it will be rewarded in game.

For story-based or non-tactical games, get in the habit of rolling at random times out of players sight. This keeps them from knowing if you are rolling e.g. a perception check, or just casually rolling. It also lets you fudge rolls if you need to, to keep the story rolling and everyone having fun. For tactical games, everything should be above-board, so players can make good decisions, and have confidence in the fairness of the game.
